label: Which part of the CIA triad a scenario actually damages

mentor.diagnosis: You answered with the element that feels most serious rather than the one the scenario describes. Confidentiality is the reflex answer and is frequently not what was lost.
contrast: Someone who should not see the data sees it
A readable backup tape leaves the building
The data is altered, whether or not anyone read it
Ransomware encrypting files: the data is intact but unusable and altered
Authorised users cannot reach it when needed
A DDoS, a failed disk, or an accidental deletion with no backup
The actor can plausibly deny having acted
A shared admin account: nobody can prove who did it
mentor.rule: Ask what the authorised user lost. If they cannot get to it, availability. If what they get back is wrong, integrity. If someone else got a copy, confidentiality.
mentor.tell: Outage, deletion, corruption, encryption by ransomware, or a shared account with no individual accountability.
mentor.trap: Ransomware is commonly answered as a confidentiality failure. Unless the attacker also exfiltrated the data, the loss is availability and integrity: you still have the bytes and can neither read nor trust them.

label: Policy engine vs policy administrator vs policy enforcement point, and adaptive identity

mentor.diagnosis: You treated the zero trust components as one system. They are deliberately split so that the thing making the decision is not the thing enforcing it.
contrast: The user, service or device requesting access
Decides: evaluates policy and signals, returns grant or deny
Communicates the decision and establishes or tears down the session
Sits in the traffic path and actually allows or blocks
Adjusts the requirement using context: device posture, location, behaviour, risk
mentor.rule: The engine decides, the administrator conveys and sets up the session, the enforcement point is the gate in the traffic. Deciding and enforcing are separate on purpose.
mentor.tell: A stem describing where a decision is made versus where traffic is blocked, or access requirements changing with context.
mentor.trap: Policy engine and policy administrator are easily swapped. The engine is the brain making the verdict; the administrator is the messenger that acts on it and manages the session.

mentor.diagnosis: You assumed authentication always means a person proving who they are. A large share of authentication in a real environment is one machine proving itself to another, with no human present.
contrast: Certificates, machine accounts, API keys, mutual TLS
Know, have, are, somewhere you are
Possession of a private key, or a secret provisioned to the device
A stolen key or an unrotated service credential in a repository
mentor.rule: If no human is present at the moment of authentication, it is a system authenticating, and the controls are certificates and key management rather than MFA prompts.
mentor.tell: Server-to-server calls, 802.1X for devices, mutual TLS, scheduled jobs, or anything described as happening overnight.
mentor.trap: Proposing multifactor authentication for a service account. There is nobody to present a second factor, which is why machine identity relies on certificates and short-lived credentials instead.

label: Honeypot vs honeynet vs honeyfile vs honeytoken

mentor.diagnosis: You matched on the word honey and guessed by scale. They differ by what the decoy is: a host, a network, a file, or a single piece of data.
contrast: A single decoy system with no production purpose
Someone is probing or exploiting, and how
A whole decoy network of them
Lateral movement and attacker behaviour at scale
A bait file that should never be opened
Someone is browsing where they should not be
A fake credential or record planted in real data
Exactly where your data went when it surfaces elsewhere
mentor.rule: Any interaction with a decoy is suspicious by definition, because nothing legitimate has a reason to touch it. That near-zero false positive rate is the entire value.
mentor.tell: A stem about detecting an intruder already inside, or about identifying which dataset was leaked.
mentor.trap: Honeytoken is the one people miss. A fake customer record with a unique address or a fake API key tells you which copy of a database leaked, the moment someone uses it.

label: Infrared, pressure, microwave and ultrasonic sensors, and deterrence vs detection

mentor.diagnosis: You picked a sensor by name recognition. Each detects a different physical phenomenon, and several of the physical controls in this objective deter rather than detect.
contrast: Heat signature of a body, so it needs a temperature difference
Weight or force on a surface, such as a floor mat
Reflected microwaves, sensing motion through some materials
Reflected sound waves, sensing movement in a volume
Detects and records; deters when visibly present
Removes the cover darkness provides, and makes other controls work
Physical obstruction of vehicles or people
The only control that can assess a situation and decide
Two interlocking doors that stop tailgating
mentor.rule: Sensors detect a phenomenon. Ask which phenomenon the scenario offers: body heat, weight, motion through a wall, or movement in a room.
mentor.tell: A stem naming a condition such as a cold room, a surface that must not be stepped on, or detection through a partition.
mentor.trap: Infrared needs a thermal contrast. In an environment near body temperature it degrades badly, which is the detail exam questions use to rule it out.

label: Gap analysis vs audit vs risk assessment

mentor.diagnosis: You read gap analysis as a general word for finding problems. It has a specific shape: current state measured against a defined desired state, producing the distance between them.
contrast: Where you are against where you intend to be, usually a framework or target maturity
A list of differences and the work to close them
Practice against a standard or policy, independently
An opinion on compliance, with findings
Threats and vulnerabilities against assets and impact
Systems against a database of known flaws
mentor.rule: A gap analysis needs a target. Without a defined desired state there is no gap to measure, only observations.
mentor.tell: Adopting a framework, preparing for certification, or a stated intention to reach a maturity level.
mentor.trap: An audit also produces findings, so the two look alike. The difference is independence and intent: an audit judges compliance, a gap analysis plans improvement.
